strengths: The paper utilizes a novel method for estimation of the difference in the value functions using the inverse of the preference functions.
It is able to prove local convergence for a non-deterministic MDP.
The paper is well laid out and easy to read.
The paper presents theoretical guarantees for zero-order optimization algorithm for RLHF.
The methods ZPG and ZBCPG work for a general class of link functions (beyond the BT-model) and stochastic dynamics as well.

Theoretical sample complexity and convergence rates that give an idea of the dependence on the number of human preferences needed, and prove convergence exists. I have not checked the proofs in detail.
The proposed algorithms are interesting, at least from a theoretical viewpoint
The paper is overall clearly and well written
There is a nice discussion of the technical difficulties for proving their results, which is quite helpful
The provided theoretical results sound plausible (some questions about the proofs of Thm1 though, and Thm 2 has not been double-checked)
weaknesses: The established local convergence with a sample complexity of $\epsilon^{-5}$ is a significant limitation.
The current literature, specifically Xie et al. (2024), has already demonstrated global convergence with a better sample complexity of $\epsilon^{-2}$.

The key issue is the lack of a clear justification for why this work is an improvement, given that the existing results provide stronger guarantees and better sample complexity, even if it is in a more restricted setting.

The practical implications of local convergence, especially in high-dimensional policy spaces common in RLHF, are unclear, as the convergence region could be very small and difficult to reach in practice.
The $\epsilon^{-5}$ sample complexity is quite high, raising concerns about the practical applicability of the method, especially when compared to methods with better sample complexities.
Even though the paper's method for estimating the difference in value functions is novel, the lack of global convergence and the higher sample complexity make the contribution questionable.

The paper needs to provide a compelling argument as to why local convergence is a sufficiently strong result in the context of current literature, and why the novel method justifies the weaker convergence guarantees and higher sample complexity.
The novelty of the method alone is not sufficient to overcome the limitations in convergence guarantees and sample complexity.
The idea of applying zero-order optimization is not novel. Similar ideas have been extensively studied in the deep RL literature.
Much literature reference is missing from discussion.
A theoretical paper like this is not very valuable to the RLHF or deep RL community.

It is not clear if the discussion here is specific to RLHF at all. Do RLHF allow us to assume additional structure on the rewards or the parameter space? No such discussion is furthered in the paper - in regular RL or deep RL setups, the same algorithmic discussions apply.
As a result, the paper is not really a RLHF specific algorithm, the algorithm itself has been extensively studied in the RL literature as well.
There is no empirical backup of the results at all, not even tabular experiments.

I think a theoretical paper in its current form like this would not offer too much additional value to the field of RLHF or deep RL. Certain amount of experimentation is warranted, and in the case of RLHF, it is also interesting to see if the algorithm can work at all and how it compares with REINFORCE / PPO.
ZPG and ZBCPG do not work directly from an offline dataset like DPO can; they require online human preferences for the current samples.

Comparing ZPG to online DPO, it seems that ZPG requires more trajectory samples (i.e. more forward passes) because you need multiple perturbations, which is multiple times more costly than online DPO.
Zero-th order methods may be slower than gradient-based methods, especially for very large models like LLMs.

No toy experiments. While LLM experiments would seem daunting in addition to the theoretical contribution, toy experiments in simple, stochastic domains to illustrate how DPO would fail but ZPG would work, would be a great addition to further motivate the need for a DPO alternative.
Overclaims and/or lack of discussion of the limitations of the proposed approach.

The paper assumes that $M$ humans are available for rating $N$ pairs of trajectories for each gradient step (and this must be done online, because the proposed approach is purely on-policy), which makes it hard to see any setting where this could be applicable or reasonable, and it is a strong drawback compared to more practical RLHF approaches.

The proposed algorithms seem to be new, and they are explicitly positioned as addressing shortcomings of classic RLHF or DPO, which would call for some empirical results, at least on bandits or toy MDPs (possibly comparing with classic RLHF, DPO, but also things like online DPO), but there is no such empirical study.
There are parts of the paper and of the proofs that are not totally clear, see questions.
The paper does not discuss limitations of the proposed approach (like the need to have on-policy online human raters) in sufficient detail and compare pros and cons with DPO and classic RLHF.

The claimed ability to handle stochastic transitions is unclear, especially since the focus is also mostly done on LLMs; the paper does not explain in which case we would have stochastic transitions in this context and how it is handled by the framework.
There is no KL regularization, compared to all other works for doing RLHF (and not without reason); it is unclear whether it is no longer required from a practical perspective.

The paper claims going "beyond the BT model", but the generalization is rather weak and could not handle more general preference models such as those considered for example in "Nash learning from human feedback" by Munos et al.

Given that the analyzed algorithm is not representative of practical approaches, and that the second proposed algorithm is motivated by computational aspects (memory, distributed aspect), a minimal empirical study (with the proposed algorithms, but also DPO, classic RLHF, online DPO) would be valuable, but is missing.

It is claimed (l.163) that the considered setting encompasses things like convex MDP. The authors should expand on this because they do not make the assumption that the return is sum-decomposable, and it is unclear why this would allow it to be framed as a convex function of the occupancy measure.

It would be possible to group or recall the properties and assumptions of the link function, as it is a quite central object; for example, should we not assume also that $\sigma(x) = 1 - \sigma(-x)$, or is it a consequence of what is already written? Could you also give some examples of the Lipschitz constants $L$ (Assm 2), for example for the logistic function used in Bradley-Terry?
There is a typo l. 305 (as written, the gradient is always zero, issue in the second value index).
Assm 2 and 3 use the same notation $L$ for the Lipschitz constant of $\sigma^{-1}$ and for $L$-smoothness of $V$, which is confusing; they should be distinguished or restated with distinct notation.
In Thm 1 and 2, $M$ is a function of $D$, a quantity which has never been defined; clarification is needed, especially as it is the number of human raters.
Corollary 1 doesn’t seem to be proven, even in the appendix; a proof should be provided.
At line 435, it is unclear how $\theta^*$ appears with a telescoping argument (the corresponding equation in the appendix involves $\theta_T$, which seems more logical).
Lemma 2 would be helpful to explain why the trim operator is introduced (the result would hold without the trim according to the proof).
There is a typo at line 977 (parenthesis).
At line 1014, it is unclear whether the $L$ mentioned is the same as in Assumption 3.

The end of proof of Thm 1 (lines 1104 to the end) is pretty unclear; clarification is needed for the derivation of equations 1106, 1110, 1122, and how they cover all possible gradient cases, as well as how the bounds are combined.
At line 1214, there is a missing term (or the line should be removed).
At lines 1230-1241, the reason for the factor 3 is unclear.
